title: 2  det(exp(A)) = exp(tr(A))
text:
We wish to prove that for a diagonalizable matrix A, the determinant of its exponential equals the exponential of its trace:

\det(\exp(A)) = \exp(\text{tr}(A))

We start with the definition of the exponential function for a scalar x:

\exp(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^3}{3!} + \ldots

We will extend this definition to include the exponential of a matrix A:

\exp(A) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{A^n}{n!} = 1 + A + \frac{A^2}{2!} + \frac{A^3}{3!} + \ldots

If A is diagonalizable:

A = P D P^{-1},

where P is a matrix whose column vectors are the eigenvectors of A, and D is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements are the corresponding eigenvalues.
Let’s use the equation above in the definition of the exponential:
\begin{align*}
\exp(A) &= \exp\left(P D P^{-1}\right) \\
&= 1 + P D P^{-1} + \frac{1}{2!}\left(P D \cancel{P^{-1}}\right)\left(\cancel{P} D P^{-1}\right) + \ldots \\
&= P D^2 P^{-1} + P D P^{-1} + \frac{1}{2!}P D^2 P^{-1} + \frac{1}{3!}P D^3 P^{-1} + \ldots
\end{align*}
If we left-multiply the last expression by P^{-1} and then right-multiply it by P, we get

P^{-1}\exp(A)P = 1 + D + \frac{D^2}{2!} + \frac{D^3}{3!} = \exp(D)

and then reversing the left- and right-multiplications we finally have:

\exp(A) = P \exp(D) P^{-1}.

We are almost there! Let’s take the determinant of both sides. In the step below we will use the following property of determinants: \det(XY)=\det(X)\det(Y). This can be untuitively justified by interpreting the determinant as the rescaling of a parallelogram defined by the linear transformation of a matrix. The rescaled parallelogram after the operation XY is scaled first by Y and then by X, giving the expression we need. Continuing:
\begin{align*}
\det(\exp(A)) &= \det(P \exp(D) P^{-1}) \\
&= \det(P)\det(\exp(D))\det(P^{-1}) \\
&= \cancel{\det(P)}\det(\exp(D))\cancel{\det(P^{-1})} \\
&= e^{d_1}e^{d_2}e^{d_3}\ldots \\
&= \exp(d_1+d_2+d_3+\ldots) \\
&= \exp(\text{tr}(D))
\end{align*}
Now, all we have to do is to replace the trace of D by the trace of A. Using the property of the trace of a product: \text{tr}(XY)=\text{tr}(YX):

\text{tr}(A) = \text{tr}(P D P^{-1}) = \text{tr}(\cancel{P^{-1}P} D) = \text{tr}(D).

Finally:

\det(\exp(A)) = \exp(\text{tr}(A))

and that concludes the proof. \blacksquare

title: 3  conjugation
text:
I’d like to thank Adam Frank for his blog post on axiomtutor.com for helping me grasp intuitively the concept of conjugation.
Conjugation represents the idea that one operation can be seen from two different points of view. I’ll start with a concrete example.
Say that k represents a reflection across the x-axis, and g represents a counter-clockwise rotation by an arbitrary angle \theta. See below these two operations applied on a heart shape.


import libraries
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.patches import Arc, RegularPolygon
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from numpy import radians as rad




define useful functions
def drawCirc(ax,radius,centX,centY,angle_,theta2_,color_='black',linewidth=3):
    #========Line
    arc = Arc([centX,centY],radius,radius,angle=angle_,
          theta1=0,theta2=theta2_,capstyle='round',linestyle='-',lw=linewidth,color=color_)
    ax.add_patch(arc)


    #========Create the arrow head
    endX=centX+(radius/2)*np.cos(rad(theta2_+angle_)) #Do trig to determine end position
    endY=centY+(radius/2)*np.sin(rad(theta2_+angle_))
    
    ax.add_patch(
        RegularPolygon(
            (endX, endY),
            numVertices=3,
            radius=radius/5,
            orientation=rad(angle_ + theta2_),
            color=color_
        )
    )




define transformations
red = 'xkcd:vermillion'
blue = 'xkcd:cerulean'
t = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 100)
x = 16* (np.sin(t)) ** 3
y = 13* np.cos(t) - 5 * np.cos(2*t) - 2 * np.cos(3*t) - np.cos(4*t)
heart = np.array([x, y])
flip_x = np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]])
def rotate(theta):
    return np.array([[np.cos(theta), -np.sin(theta)], [np.sin(theta), np.cos(theta)]])
heart_x = flip_x @ heart
theta = np.atan(0.5)
heart_minus_theta = rotate(-theta) @ heart
heart_minus_theta_flipped = flip_x @ heart_minus_theta
heart_minus_theta_flipped_plus_theta = rotate(theta) @ heart_minus_theta_flipped
x_oblique_axis = np.array([-25, 25])
y_oblique_axis = 0.5 * x_oblique_axis
oblique_axis = np.array([x_oblique_axis, y_oblique_axis])
oblique_axis_minus_theta = rotate(-theta) @ oblique_axis
oblique_axis_minus_theta_plus_theta = rotate(theta) @ oblique_axis_minus_theta




plot k and g applied to a heart shape
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, sharey=True, figsize=(8, 4))
ax[0].plot(heart[0], heart[1], color=red)
ax[0].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[0].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[0].set_aspect('equal')
ax[0].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title='heart', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)

ax[1].plot(heart_x[0], heart_x[1], color=red)
ax[1].axhline(0, color=blue, lw=2)
ax[1].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[1].set_aspect('equal')
ax[1].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title='k: reflection across x-axis', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)

heart_15 = rotate(np.pi/12) @ heart
ax[2].plot(heart_15[0], heart_15[1], color=red)
ax[2].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[2].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[2].set_aspect('equal')
ax[2].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title=r'g: ccw rotation by $\theta$', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)
drawCirc(ax[2],radius=10,centX=0,centY=0,angle_=270,theta2_=150, color_=blue);









Because we are dealing with operations on a 2d plane, both k and g can be represented as 2\times2 matrices:

k =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & -1
\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
g =
\begin{pmatrix}
\cos(\theta) & -\sin(\theta) \\
\sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta)
\end{pmatrix}

What if we want to make a reflection of the heart shape across a different axis? In the graph below, the first panel on the left shows a reflection axis that is rotated by an angle \theta from the x-axis. With a little ingenuity, I don’t need to define a new reflection operation. Instead, I can use the existing reflection operation k and the rotation operation g to achieve the same effect.


conjugation of k and g applied to a heart shape
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, sharey=True, figsize=(10, 3))
ax[0].plot(heart[0], heart[1], color=red)
ax[0].plot(oblique_axis[0], oblique_axis[1], color=blue, lw=2)
ax[0].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[0].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[0].set_aspect('equal')
ax[0].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title='heart', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)

ax[1].plot(heart_minus_theta[0], heart_minus_theta[1], color=red)
ax[1].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[1].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[1].plot(oblique_axis_minus_theta[0], oblique_axis_minus_theta[1], color=blue, lw=2)
ax[1].set_aspect('equal')
ax[1].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title=r'1: apply $g^{-1}$' + "\n" + r'rotate $-\theta$', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)

ax[2].plot(heart_minus_theta_flipped[0], heart_minus_theta_flipped[1], color=red)
ax[2].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[2].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[2].plot(oblique_axis_minus_theta[0], oblique_axis_minus_theta[1], color=blue, lw=2)
ax[2].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title=r'2: apply $k$' + "\n" + r'flip across x axis', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)
ax[2].set_aspect('equal')

ax[3].plot(heart_minus_theta_flipped_plus_theta[0], heart_minus_theta_flipped_plus_theta[1], color=red)
ax[3].plot(heart[0], heart[1], color=red, alpha=0.2, ls=":")
ax[3].axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[3].axvline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
ax[3].plot(oblique_axis_minus_theta_plus_theta[0], oblique_axis_minus_theta_plus_theta[1], color=blue, lw=2)
ax[3].set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y', title=r'3: apply $g$' + "\n" + r'rotate $\theta$', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis)
ax[3].set_aspect('equal');










We rotate the whole plane by an angle -\theta, which rotates the reflection axis (blue) to coincide with the x-axis (2nd panel). This is equivalent to applying the inverse of the rotation operation g^{-1} to the heart shape.
Then we reflect the (rotated) heart shape across the x-axis (3rd panel). This is simply applying the reflection operation k to the rotated heart shape.
Finally, we rotate the whole plane back by an angle \theta (4th panel). This is equivalent to applying the rotation operation g to the reflected heart shape. You can check the result by comparing the solid red curve with the original heart shape shown with a dotted line.

To sum up: apply g^{-1}, then k, then g. Let’s call the resulting operation k', which is said to be a conjugate of k by g:

k' = g k g^{-1}.

Now let’s see the same thing from a slightly different perspective. If k means reflecting across the x-axis, then k' can also be interpreted as reflecting across the x-axis, but in a rotated coordinate system. See below, the usual axes x and y are used in the panel on the left, while a rotated coordinate system by \theta is used in the panel on the right.


conjugation of k and g applied to a heart shape
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True, figsize=(6, 3))

ax[0].plot(heart[0], heart[1], color=red)
ax[0].plot(heart_x[0], heart_x[1], color=red, alpha=0.2)
ax[0].axhline(0, color=blue, lw=2)
ax[0].set_aspect('equal')
ax[0].set(title='usual coordinate system', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis, xticks=[], yticks=[])
ax[0].annotate("", xy=(20, 0), xytext=(0, 0), fontsize=10, color="black", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", facecolor='black', lw=4, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0),)
ax[0].annotate("", xy=(0, 20), xytext=(0, 0), fontsize=10, color="black", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", facecolor='black', lw=4, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0),)
ax[0].text(20, 1, r'$x$', fontsize=16, color="black")
ax[0].text(1, 20, r'$y$', fontsize=16, color="black")

ex = np.array([[20,0]])
x_prime = rotate(theta) @ ex.T
why = np.array([[0,20]])
y_prime = rotate(theta) @ why.T

ax[1].plot(heart[0], heart[1], color=red)
ax[1].plot(heart_minus_theta_flipped_plus_theta[0], heart_minus_theta_flipped_plus_theta[1], color=red, alpha=0.2)
ax[1].plot(oblique_axis[0], oblique_axis[1], color=blue, lw=2)
ax[1].set_aspect('equal')
ax[1].set(title='rotated coordinate system', xlim=x_oblique_axis, ylim=x_oblique_axis, xticks=[], yticks=[])
ax[1].annotate("", xy=x_prime, xytext=(0, 0), fontsize=10, color="black", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", facecolor='black', lw=4, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0),)
ax[1].annotate("", xy=y_prime, xytext=(0, 0), fontsize=10, color="black", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", facecolor='black', lw=4, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0),)
ax[1].text(15, 10, r"$x'$", fontsize=16, color="black")
ax[1].text(-7, 18, r"$y'$", fontsize=16, color="black");









The rotated coordinate system is defined by unit vectors x' and y' which are exactly the column vectors of the rotation matrix g!
So, another way to interpret the conjugation k' = g k g^{-1} is that it represents the same operation k (reflection across the x-axis), but in a rotated coordinate system defined by g.
The idea of conjugation is very general and can be applied to any operation, not just reflections. The one requirement is that the operation g must be invertible, so that we can apply g^{-1} to reverse the effect of g.
The underlying principle behind this generality is the “change-of-basis” formula. If M is the matrix of an operation k in a given basis, and g is an invertible matrix whose column vectors define a new basis, then

g^{-1}Mg

is the matrix of the same operator written in the basis whose vectors are the columns of g.
Conjugation by g preserves many properties of the operation k.

The determinant of k' is the same as the determinant of k.
The trace of k' is the same as the trace of k.
The eigenvalues of k' are the same as the eigenvalues of k. (The eigenvectors are rotated by g).
The conjugation of a bracket of two operations is the same as the bracket of the conjugated operations: \begin{align*}
[k, l]' &= g [k, l] g^{-1} \\
&= g (kl - lk) g^{-1} \\
&= gklg^{-1} - glkg^{-1} \\
&= gkg^{-1}glg^{-1} - glg^{-1}gkg^{-1} \\
&= (gkg^{-1})(glg^{-1}) - (glg^{-1})(gkg^{-1}) \\
&= [gkg^{-1}, glg^{-1}] \\
&= [k', l']
\end{align*}

title: 4  polarization and Jones vectors
text:
4.1 the electric field, stripped down
this page is under construction
I’m working through eigenchris’ Spinors for Beginners series, and I want to use this chapter to rebuild, in my own words, the first “physical” example he gives of a spinor: the polarization of a light wave. The reason I find this example so convincing as a starting point is that there is nothing quantum about it. A spinor shows up here as a convenient bookkeeping device for a completely classical phenomenon, which tells me that whatever makes something “a spinor” cannot be about quantum mechanics per se — it has to be about how an object transforms.
A plane electromagnetic wave travelling along z has an electric field confined to the xy-plane (it’s a transverse wave, so there’s no z-component to worry about). Writing the y-component of a vertically polarized wave as
E_y(z,t) = A\cos(\omega t - kz + \phi),
I can trade the cosine for a complex exponential and carry the real-part instruction around implicitly — this is the same trick used everywhere in AC circuit theory and optics:
E_y(z,t) = \operatorname{Re}\Big[ A\, e^{i\phi}\, e^{i(\omega t - kz)} \Big].
The combination A e^{i\phi} is the only part of this expression that carries information about this particular wave as opposed to waves in general — the factor e^{i(\omega t - kz)} is shared by every wave with this frequency and direction of travel, so it can be factored out and ignored. What’s left, once I do the same thing for a horizontally polarized wave and add the two together, is a 2-component object:
\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} A_H e^{i\phi_H} \\ A_V e^{i\phi_V} \end{pmatrix}.
This is the Jones vector. It’s a complete description of the polarization state of the wave — nothing about the “actual” travelling wave survives in it, only amplitudes and relative phases.

title: 4  polarization and Jones vectors
text:
4.2 six special points
If I restrict myself to unit-length Jones vectors (an overall scale doesn’t change the polarization — more on that below), a few combinations have names worth remembering, because they’re the ones that come up over and over in optics:








name
vector
picture




horizontal H
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}
oscillates along x


vertical V
\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}
oscillates along y


diagonal D
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
45° line


anti-diagonal A
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
-45° line


left circular L
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}
field traces a circle, left-handed


right circular R
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix}
field traces a circle, right-handed



I like deriving L and R by brute force instead of taking them on faith: plug \mathbf{J}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix} into the travelling-wave formula, set z=0, \omega=1, and just walk t through 0,\pi/2,\pi,3\pi/2. The real part of the field visits (1,0) \to (0,-1) \to (-1,0) \to (0,1) — a clockwise circle when viewed looking into the direction of travel, which is “left circular” by the optics convention (point your left thumb along the direction of travel; your fingers curl the way the field rotates).

title: 4  polarization and Jones vectors
section: 4.3 what a Jones vector is not allowed to know
text:
4.3 what a Jones vector is not allowed to know
Two facts turn out to be the whole story later on:

Overall phase is invisible. Multiplying \mathbf{J} by e^{i\chi} for any real \chi just shifts the wave along z — the polarization itself is untouched. So \mathbf{J} and e^{i\chi}\mathbf{J} describe the same physical polarization state.
Overall scale is invisible (once we care only about polarization and not intensity). Doubling \mathbf{J} doubles the brightness, not the shape of the polarization ellipse.

Together, these say that a polarization state is really an equivalence class of Jones vectors under \mathbf{J} \sim c\,\mathbf{J} for any nonzero complex c. That is a much more interesting statement than it looks — it’s exactly the equivalence relation that defines the complex projective line \mathbb{CP}^1, and it’s the reason a 2-component complex object ends up needing only two real numbers (a point on a sphere) to specify it. I’ll come back to this once the same pattern shows up for quantum spin states — chasing an identical piece of algebra across two completely different physical settings is, to me, the most convincing argument that “spinor” names a real mathematical structure rather than a quantum-mechanics curiosity.

title: 5  rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere
text:
5.1 borrowing the logic from real rotations
this page is under construction
Having written polarization states as Jones vectors in the previous chapter, the natural next question is: what matrices are allowed to act on them? Physically, a wave plate rotates one polarization into another by delaying the vertical component relative to the horizontal one by some phase. Mathematically, I want to find the group of matrices that can represent all physically realizable polarization changes, and understand why it has to be SU(2) rather than something bigger or smaller.
Before touching complex vectors, it’s worth re-deriving the familiar case: what matrices R preserve the length of a real 3D vector v? Length-squared is v^\top v, and requiring (Rv)^\top(Rv) = v^\top v for every v forces
R^\top R = I.
These are the orthogonal matrices, O(3). Taking determinants of both sides gives (\det R)^2 = 1, so \det R = \pm 1: reflections get a -1, rotations get a +1. Restricting to \det R = +1 is what “special” means, and that’s SO(3).

title: 5  rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere
section: 5.2 the same logic, with complex entries
text:
5.2 the same logic, with complex entries
A Jones vector has complex entries, so “length” has to mean \mathbf{J}^\dagger\mathbf{J} (Hermitian conjugate, not plain transpose) or I’d get a complex number out of a thing that’s supposed to be a probability-like intensity. Demanding that a matrix U preserve this quantity for every \mathbf{J} gives, by the identical argument as above,

U^\dagger U = I,

the defining property of a unitary matrix. The 2\times2 unitary matrices form the group U(2). Taking the determinant of U^\dagger U = I gives |\det U|^2 = 1, so \det U is not forced to be \pm1 this time — it can be any unit-modulus complex number e^{i\theta}.
This is the first place where the complex case genuinely differs from the real one, and it matters: a generic U(2) matrix carries an unavoidable overall phase in its determinant. But I already know from the previous chapter that overall phase is physically invisible for Jones vectors. So U(2) has redundancy built into it — many different U(2) matrices produce the same physical rotation of the polarization ellipse, differing only by a phase that gets thrown away anyway.
crumbs: 5  rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere

title: 5  rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere
text:
5.3 picking a unique representative: SU(2)
To remove the redundancy, I can always rescale any U \in U(2) by e^{-i\theta/2} (where \theta = \arg\det U) to force its determinant to be exactly 1, without changing the physical transformation it represents. The matrices with

U^\dagger U = I, \qquad \det U = 1

form SU(2), and this is the group that acts on Jones vectors (and, as the next chapter shows, on quantum spin states) without any leftover ambiguity beyond the one we already knew about and chose to ignore.
crumbs: 5  rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere

title: 5  rotating Jones vectors: U(2), SU(2), and the Poincaré sphere
text:
5.4 the angle-doubling, finally made precise
Here’s the calculation that I think earns the name “spinor.” Physically, H and V polarizations are 90° apart in real space. But a half-wave plate — the device that swaps H \leftrightarrow V — corresponds to a full 180° rotation of the Jones vector on the Poincaré sphere (it has to go H \to D \to V, a half-circle). Chasing this through:

\text{physical angle } \theta \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{Poincaré-sphere angle } 2\theta.

This is why the SU(2) matrices that implement wave-plate rotations are conventionally written with half-angles:

U(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\theta/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{i\theta/2} \end{pmatrix}

for rotation about the H/V axis, and structurally similar matrices (built from Pauli matrices, which will show up again when we get to Lie algebras) for rotations about the other two axes of the sphere.
The thing I want to hold onto from this chapter is where the factor of two actually comes from. It isn’t some mysterious property bolted onto spinors by fiat — it falls straight out of the fact that (-1)\cdot\mathbf{J} and \mathbf{J} are the same physical state. A rotation that looks like “half a turn” on the sphere of physical polarization ellipses is a “full turn” on the sphere of Jones-vector directions, because the latter sphere has already glued antipodal points together. Once you see the gluing, the factor of two stops being surprising.

title: 6  Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states
text:
6.1 what the experiment actually shows
this page is under construction
The striking thing about this chapter, for me, is not the physics of the Stern-Gerlach experiment itself — it’s that once the dust settles, the mathematics is identical to the Jones-vector story. Same two-component complex columns, same invisibility of overall phase and scale, same SU(2) rotation group, same angle-doubling. Two completely different physical setups (a classical EM wave through crystal optics, and a beam of silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnet) land on exactly the same piece of linear algebra. That convergence is the real argument that spinors are a mathematical structure worth naming, not a quirk of quantum theory.
Send neutral silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnetic field and measure their deflection. Classically, you’d expect a continuous spread of outcomes (every orientation of a tiny bar magnet deflects by a different amount). What you actually see is two spots, nothing in between. That’s the experimental fact that forces angular momentum — specifically, the un-paired electron’s intrinsic spin — to be quantized.

title: 6  Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states
text:
6.2 bra-ket bookkeeping
Quantum states live in an abstract vector space, written as kets |\psi\rangle, with Hermitian conjugates (bras) \langle\psi|. Born’s rule says the probability of measuring a system prepared in state |a\rangle to collapse into state |b\rangle is

P(a \to b) = |\langle b | a \rangle|^2.

Running the Stern-Gerlach beam through a \hat z-oriented magnet and then a second \hat z-magnet shows |{+z}\rangle and |{-z}\rangle are orthogonal, unit-norm states — exactly as expected, since “up” and “down” are mutually exclusive outcomes.
crumbs: 6  Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states

title: 6  Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states
section: 6.3 the x and y states are where it gets interesting
text:
6.3 the x and y states are where it gets interesting
Rotate the apparatus to point along \hat x and repeat: you again get two outcomes, |{+x}\rangle and |{-x}\rangle, each orthogonal and unit-norm. But now feed a |{+x}\rangle beam into a \hat z-oriented magnet, and you get a 50/50 split. Born’s rule then pins down

|{+x}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle + |{-z}\rangle\big), \qquad
|{-x}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle - |{-z}\rangle\big).

Repeating along \hat y forces complex coefficients — real numbers alone can’t give a second pair of states that’s simultaneously 50/50 against z and orthogonal to the x-states already claimed:

|{+y}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle + i|{-z}\rangle\big), \qquad
|{-y}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(|{+z}\rangle - i|{-z}\rangle\big).

Lay these six states side by side with the six Jones vectors H,V,D,A,L,R from the optics chapter and the dictionary is exact, component for component. That’s not a loose analogy — the underlying linear algebra doesn’t know or care which physical system it’s describing.
crumbs: 6  Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states

title: 6  Stern-Gerlach and quantum spin states
section: 6.4 why U(2) is “too big” here as well
text:
6.4 why U(2) is “too big” here as well
Just as with Jones vectors, rotating a spin state with a unitary matrix leaves Born’s rule probabilities unchanged if the matrix is multiplied by an overall phase — the phase exits the inner product via the bra’s complex conjugation and squares away to 1. So U(2) over-describes the physical rotations, and we again cut the redundancy by demanding \det U = 1, landing on SU(2) as the group that rotates spin states around the Bloch sphere (the quantum-mechanics name for the same sphere optics calls the Poincaré sphere).
The payoff is the same angle-doubling as before, but now it’s worth stating in the language this book is named after: physical rotations in 3D space form SO(3), and the matrices that correctly transform spin-\tfrac12 states form SU(2). The map SU(2) \to SO(3) that sends a spinor rotation to the physical rotation it induces is exactly two-to-one — both U and -U in SU(2) produce the same rotation in SO(3), for the same reason \mathbf{J} and -\mathbf{J} represent the same polarization. SU(2) is the double cover of SO(3). Everything in this chapter and the last one is the two-to-one covering map, worked out by hand in a specific low-dimensional case before we have the Lie-theory language to say it in one line.

title: 7  flagpoles, and spinors as points on a projective line
text:
7.1 throwing away two of the four real numbers
this page is under construction
The last two chapters kept running into the same two facts: a spinor \mathbf{J}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\end{pmatrix} doesn’t care about an overall phase, and it doesn’t care about an overall (nonzero) scale. I want to take those two facts seriously as a definition rather than as a pair of annoying caveats, because doing so explains, in one stroke, both why a spinor can be drawn as a point on a sphere and why that sphere has the angle-doubling property baked in from the start.
\alpha and \beta are each complex, so naively a spinor needs four real numbers. But since \mathbf J and c\mathbf J (any nonzero complex c) are the same spinor, I’m free to pick c = 1/\alpha and normalize the top entry to exactly 1:
\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\end{pmatrix} \;\sim\; \begin{pmatrix}1\\ \beta/\alpha\end{pmatrix}.
Everything that matters about the spinor is contained in the single complex number \beta/\alpha — two real numbers, not four. That’s exactly enough to specify a point on a sphere (longitude and latitude), which is why the Poincaré/Bloch sphere picture works at all: it isn’t a visualization trick bolted on afterward, it’s a direct consequence of quotienting by an overall complex factor.

title: 7  flagpoles, and spinors as points on a projective line
section: 7.2 putting the two discarded numbers back as a flagpole
text:
7.2 putting the two discarded numbers back as a flagpole
It still feels wasteful to throw \arg(\alpha) and |\alpha| away completely, so eigenchris’ picture keeps them visible: draw the spinor not as a bare point on the sphere, but as a flagpole planted at that point. The length of the pole encodes the overall scale we’re ignoring, and the angle of a little flag at the top encodes the overall phase we’re ignoring. Changing either one moves the flag or stretches the pole, but the point where the pole meets the sphere — the only part that is physically meaningful — never moves. I like this picture because it keeps the discarded information in view instead of pretending it never existed; it’s a visual reminder that “spinor” is a specific quotient, not a mysterious new kind of number.

title: 7  flagpoles, and spinors as points on a projective line
section: 7.3 real projective line first, because it’s easier to draw
text:
7.3 real projective line first, because it’s easier to draw
To see why this quotient construction forces the angle-doubling, it helps to step down to real numbers first. Take the xy-plane, put a screen at x=1, and project every point (x,y) along the ray through the origin to wherever that ray crosses the screen, landing at (1, y/x). The destination depends only on the ratio y/x — so scaling (x,y) by any nonzero real number doesn’t move the projected point. This quotient space is the real projective line, \mathbb{RP}^1.
Two features of this projection matter a lot:

Points with x=0 never hit the screen — they get sent to a single point at infinity, which closes the line up into a loop.
Two points on opposite sides of a circle centered at the origin — i.e. related by an overall factor of -1 — land on the same point of the screen, since y/x is unchanged by flipping the sign of both coordinates.

That second bullet is the whole mechanism. Walk a point halfway around the circle and its projection sweeps across the entire screen (through infinity and back); walk it the rest of the way around and the projection repeats the same sweep. One trip around the circle is two trips around the projective line. This is the angle-doubling, with all the physics stripped away — it’s pure projective geometry.

title: 7  flagpoles, and spinors as points on a projective line
section: 7.4 the complex version is the spinor sphere
text:
7.4 the complex version is the spinor sphere
Doing the identical construction with a pair of complex numbers (\alpha,\beta), projecting via the ratio \beta/\alpha, gives the complex projective line, \mathbb{CP}^1. It can’t be drawn as literally as the real case (it would need four real dimensions), but the quotient is visualized the same way physicists already draw it: as the Riemann sphere, with \alpha=0 sent to the north pole (“point at infinity”) and antipodal-under-scaling points identified. The Poincaré sphere and the Bloch sphere are the same object wearing different hats — both are \mathbb{CP}^1, decorated with whichever six physical states (polarizations, or spin states) happen to sit at convenient locations on it.
So the cleanest definition I can give myself, after four chapters of examples, is: a spinor is a point on \mathbb{CP}^1, i.e. an equivalence class of nonzero pairs of complex numbers under overall complex scaling. Every angle-doubling fact we ran into — in optics, in Stern-Gerlach, and in the abstract SU(2) \to SO(3) covering map — is a restatement of the fact that this quotient turns one full loop into two. The next step up the staircase is to stop treating that factor of two as special to low dimensions and instead build it out of Clifford algebras, where it will appear for free in any dimension.
